0.title: Haggai: Consider Your Ways
0.overview:
The message. Haggai tells a tired, distracted people to put God first, and promises that God is with them when they do. They had come home from exile to rebuild the LORD’s house, and then stopped, saying “the time has not yet come” (1:2) while they made their own homes comfortable. God answers, “Consider your ways” (1:5, 7): their thin harvests are not bad luck but his call to turn round. When they obey, the rebuke turns to promise: “I am with you” (1:13); “My Spirit remains in your midst” (2:5); “from this day on I will bless you” (2:19). And the small, unimpressive temple they are building is not the end of the story, because God means to fill his house with a glory greater than Solomon’s.

Background: the writer. We know almost nothing about Haggai beyond his messages. The book calls him simply “Haggai the prophet” (1:1) and “the messenger of the LORD” (1:13), and gives no father or home town. Ezra records that “the prophets, Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied to the Jews who were in Judah and Jerusalem” (Ezra 5:1), and that the builders “prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo” (Ezra 6:14). The book speaks of Haggai in the third person, so it may have been put in order by Haggai himself or by someone close to him; either way, this commentary reads it as a faithful record of what God said through him, written down soon after.

When and where. In 587 or 586 BC the Babylonians burned Solomon’s temple. In 539 BC Babylon fell to Cyrus of Persia, who let the exiles go home and rebuild. The first returners laid the temple’s foundation, met opposition from their neighbours, and stopped (Ezra 3–4). For some sixteen years the site lay unfinished. Then, in “the second year of Darius the king” (1:1), 520 BC, Haggai spoke. Darius I had taken the Persian throne in 522 BC and spent his first years putting down revolts across the empire; a world that seemed to shake gives point to God’s words, “I will shake all nations” (2:7). Every one of Haggai’s four messages is dated, all within about four months of that year, and the temple was finished in 516 or 515 BC (Ezra 6:15).

The first hearers. Judah was now a small district of the Persian empire, with Jerusalem still half in ruins. Its two leaders were Zerubbabel, the governor, a grandson of King Jehoiachin and so of David’s royal line, and Joshua the high priest. The people were poor: drought and blight had struck their crops (1:10–11; 2:17), and what they earned seemed to go into “a bag with holes” (1:6). They were also discouraged. Some older people could remember Solomon’s temple, and the new one seemed “as nothing” beside it (2:3). Haggai’s fellow prophet Zechariah began preaching to the same people two months after him.

How to read it. Haggai is prophecy, but plain prose rather than poetry, and very practical. Like the earlier prophets, it reads the people’s hardships in the light of the covenant God made with them “when you came out of Egypt” (2:5), in which he had warned that disobedience would bring failed harvests. Its promises often reach further than the day they were spoken: the shaking of heaven and earth and the glory of the latter house were only partly seen in 515 BC, and look on to something greater.

How the book makes its case. The book is four dated messages. The first (1:1–15) is a rebuke: God’s house lies in ruins while the people live in “paneled houses” (1:4), so he calls them to consider their ways and build. Leaders and people obey, God stirs up their spirit, and within twenty-three days they are at work. The second (2:1–9) is encouragement for the discouraged: “Be strong… Work, for I am with you” (2:4), with the promise that “the latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former” (2:9). The third (2:10–19) is a lesson from the priests: holiness does not pass by touch, but uncleanness does, so their work cannot make them clean; yet God will bless them from this day. The fourth (2:20–23) is for Zerubbabel alone: when God overthrows the thrones of the nations, he will make him “like a signet ring, for I have chosen you” (2:23). The order is the gospel’s order: a call to repent, then grace to those who turn, and a promise that looks beyond them.

Did the promise to Zerubbabel fail? Zerubbabel never became king, and the thrones of the nations were not overthrown in his day; Persia went on ruling. Some therefore conclude that Haggai’s hopes were simply disappointed. But the signet ring answers a word spoken earlier: God had said that even if Zerubbabel’s grandfather Jehoiachin, called Coniah, “were the signet ring on my right hand, yet I would tear you off” (Jeremiah 22:24). Haggai says the ring is being put back on. The promise was not that Zerubbabel himself would rule, but that God had not cast off David’s line. This commentary’s view is that the promise was kept, as Matthew shows when he traces that line through “Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel” (Matthew 1:12) to Jesus.

Where it leads: to Christ. Haggai leads to Christ by promise and by pattern. The promise of greater glory was not fulfilled by gold, for the rebuilt temple was never as splendid as Solomon’s; it was fulfilled when the Son of God himself came into that very temple, which Herod had enlarged. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). He spoke of his own body as the true temple: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). The peace God promised “in this place” (2:9) is the peace Christ made by his cross, for “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). Hebrews takes up Haggai’s “Yet once more” and says the final shaking will remove all that can be shaken, so “let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Hebrews 12:28). And Zerubbabel, the chosen servant from a line that seemed finished, points to the greater Son of David, in whom “all the promises of God find their Yes” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

For us. Haggai is not a prosperity formula; God promises to meet his people’s needs, not to make them rich, and his point is priority. Jesus says it positively: “seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33). Nor is a church building God’s house today; his people are: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). So Haggai asks what gets our first time, money and strength, and exposes our favourite excuse, “not yet”. It is also gentle with those who think their work for God is small, for the One who says “Consider your ways” also says “I am with you.” Our obedience cannot make us clean, as 2:10–14 shows; only Christ can. But those he has made clean he sends to build, and his work in small hands is never small.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — This House Lies in Ruins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Putting our own comfort ahead of God’s work does not even deliver the comfort. God opens by quoting the people’s reasonable-sounding excuse, “the time has not yet come”, and sets it beside the facts: there has been time enough for panelled houses of their own while his house lies in ruins (vv. 1–4). Then he calls them, before any command, to stop and consider their ways. Everything they do is leaking: much sown and little harvested, food that does not fill, clothes that do not warm, wages dropped “into a bag with holes” (vv. 5–6). The frustration is not chance; it is God speaking.
verseByVerse.theology: When God's house is neglected for the sake of our own comfort, God can make our comforts leak away.

verseByVerse.quote: In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the LORD came by the hand of Haggai the prophet to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest: "Thus says the LORD of hosts: These people say the time has not yet come to rebuild the house of the LORD." Then the word of the LORD came by the hand of Haggai the prophet, "Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people have put off his house while finishing their own, and he names their “not yet” for what it is.

In the second year of Darius the king. Haggai is precisely dated: the first day of the sixth month of Darius’s second year, late summer 520 BC. Cyrus had let the Jews go home about eighteen years earlier, and they had returned, laid the foundation of a new temple, run into opposition, and stopped (see the introduction).

To Zerubbabel … and to Joshua. The two men named represent the two halves of the community’s life: Zerubbabel the governor, the civil leader and a descendant of David, and Joshua the high priest. The book of Ezra records that “the prophets, Haggai and Zechariah” got the work moving again (Ezra 5:1–2).

These people say the time has not yet come. The excuse is beautifully reasonable. Not “we refuse”; just: not yet. The economy is poor, the opposition is strong, the paperwork is difficult. Later. And God calls them “These people”, not “my people”: delay has put a distance between them.

Is it a time for you yourselves? God takes their own word “time” and turns it back on them: if there is no time for his house, how is there time for their own? Their paneled houses had finished interiors, wood panelling on the walls, the mark of a comfortable home. Their own building had not been postponed at all. They had money and energy; they simply spent both on themselves.

Not refused, but postponed. Most of what God asks of us is not refused outright but postponed: the conversation we should have, the giving we mean to start, the sin we intend to deal with. The test still works: look not at what we say our priorities are but at where the time and money actually went last year. That is the real list.

Is this about church buildings today? The temple was the unique place of God’s presence under the old covenant; now his people are his temple (1 Corinthians 3:16). So this is no command to fund church buildings, but its lesson stands: putting our own comfort ahead of God’s work brings emptiness (vv. 6, 9). And the temple pointed forward: Jesus called his own body the temple (John 2:19–21), for in him God came to dwell with his people, and by his Spirit he now dwells in them.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “paneled” means “covered”. It may mean roofed, so that the people had roofs over their heads while God’s house had none, or covered with fine wood, as Solomon covered the temple with cedar (1 Kings 6:9). Either way, their houses were finished and his was not.
verseByVerse.note: Work on the temple had stood still for about sixteen years, from soon after the foundation was laid until the second year of Darius (Ezra 4:4-5, 24).

verseByVerse.quote: Now, therefore, thus says the LORD of hosts: Consider your ways. You have sown much, and harvested little. You eat, but you never have enough; you drink, but you never have your fill. You clothe yourselves, but no one is warm. And he who earns wages does so to put them into a bag with holes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells his people to stop and look honestly at their lives, because everything they work for is leaking away.

Consider your ways. Literally, set your heart on your roads: stop, and look at where you are actually going. God does not begin with a command to build. He begins by asking them to think, because most of us drift into wrong priorities rather than choose them, and the first step back is an honest look.

You have sown much, and harvested little. Then the evidence, every clause an experience they had all had. Big sowing, small harvest. Meals that do not satisfy, drinks that do not cheer, clothes that do not warm. And the unforgettable image: “he who earns wages does so to put them into a bag with holes”. Anyone who has watched a salary vanish knows that bag: the car breaks, the boiler fails, the bills rise, and at the end of the month there is nothing to show for it. God is saying that this was not bad luck. He had been speaking to them through their own finances, and they had not heard.

The way back. When the honest look shows how much has gone to our own houses, the way back is not a frantic effort to make up for it but a return to the God who says, before this chapter ends, “I am with you” (v. 13). Only one man ever put his Father’s house first without fail, the one of whom it was written, “Zeal for your house will consume me” (John 2:17), and his obedience is counted as theirs for all who trust him.

What it does not mean. This passage is often misused. God is not saying that giving money to a building project guarantees prosperity. He is dealing with a specific people under a specific covenant (Israel’s covenant, which tied harvests to obedience), and his point is priority, not investment. Jesus put the same principle positively: “seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33).

How do I consider my ways? Set aside an hour with a Bible, a pen and two honest documents: your diary and your bank statement. Read them as God reads them. Where did the hours and the money actually go this month, and what came last? Name what you have postponed. Write down the one or two things you know God has asked of you and keep labelling “not yet”: the giving, the apology, the place of service, the habit of prayer. Ask why. Behind most delay is a fear or a love: fear of having less, love of comfort or of being well thought of. Pray it through. “Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!” (Psalm 139:23). Take one step this week. Haggai’s hearers went from sermon to scaffolding in twenty-three days (v. 15); choose the smallest real step and take it before the week is out. Do this without dread: the honest look is safe for those who belong to Christ, because it can uncover nothing his cross has not already covered.

Why does more never feel like enough? Haggai’s hearers would have recognised a modern finding. In 1971 the researchers, Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell, coined the phrase “hedonic treadmill” for the way we quickly get used to every gain: the pay rise, the bigger house, the new kitchen. Within months it feels normal, and we need the next thing. In Haggai’s words, “you eat, but you never have enough”. Our culture says run faster; Haggai says the leak is not in the bag but in the heart. They had panelled houses and still felt poor, asking a home and a harvest to give what only God can give. That ache is not a design fault; it is a homing instinct. So the cure in this chapter is not a better budget but a presence: “I am with you” (v. 13). Christ is the one treasure that does not wear thin with having, because he is the God the heart was made for.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s house is for his pleasure and glory, and he governs the harvests his people depend on. After a second “Consider your ways”, the command is plain and practical: go up to the hills, bring wood and build, so that God may take pleasure in his house and be glorified (vv. 7–8). Then he explains their disappointment. They looked for much and got little, because he blew it away; and the reason was his ruined house while each of them busied himself with his own (v. 9). So the heavens have held back the dew, and he has called a drought on everything their labour touches (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: God's glory, not our convenience, is the point of his house, and he governs the weather on which our harvests depend.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD of hosts: Consider your ways. Go up to the hills and bring wood and build the house, that I may take pleasure in it and that I may be glorified, says the LORD. You looked for much, and behold, it came to little. And when you brought it home, I blew it away. Why? declares the LORD of hosts. Because of my house that lies in ruins, while each of you busies himself with his own house. Therefore the heavens above you have withheld the dew, and the earth has withheld its produce. And I have called for a drought on the land and the hills, on the grain, the new wine, the oil, on what the ground brings forth, on man and beast, and on all their labors."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Build my house for my pleasure and glory, says God; your failed harvests were my doing, because each of you is busy with his own house.

Go up to the hills and bring wood. The second “Consider your ways” is followed by an ordinary instruction: go to the hills, cut wood, build. God’s work usually begins with a task anyone could describe, not with a feeling.

That I may take pleasure in it and that I may be glorified. The reason matters. The temple was not for their comfort or their national pride. God wanted a house among his people because he intended to be honoured there. Any work we do for God has the same test: is this for his pleasure and glory, or for ours?

I blew it away. God says he himself caused the disappointing harvests. This is meant to be uncomfortable. He would rather have his people poor and attentive than prosperous and indifferent.

Each of you busies himself with his own house. The diagnosis is in this clause. Not one grand act of rebellion: everyone simply attending to their own affairs, and nobody attending to God’s. The Hebrew is vivid: each one “runs” to his own house.

I have called for a drought. God says he called for a drought, as a master calls a servant. The list is thorough: grain, new wine, oil, crops, people, livestock and work itself. These were the very things the covenant had warned would fail if Israel turned from the LORD (Deuteronomy 28:38–40), so the drought was not random but a covenant message they should have been able to read.

Where God takes pleasure. The pleasure and glory God sought in a house of stone, he found perfectly in his Son: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17); “I glorified you on earth” (John 17:4). Our work pleases God not because it is impressive but because it is done in the one he delights in.

Reading hardship rightly. We should be careful not to read every hardship as a specific judgment; Job’s friends made that mistake, and Jesus corrected it (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:2–3). But we should not assume that God never speaks through circumstances either. Here he says plainly that he did.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God’s people obey his word, he gives them himself, and he supplies the very willingness to keep going. Leaders and people alike obey the voice of the LORD and the words of his prophet, and the people fear the LORD (v. 12). God answers with the shortest message in the book, “I am with you, declares the LORD” (v. 13). Then he stirs up the spirit of the governor, the high priest and all the remnant, and they come and work on his house (v. 14). The date is recorded: twenty-three days after the sermon, sixteen years of “not yet” are over (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: God meets his people's obedience with his presence, and himself supplies the will to obey.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, with all the remnant of the people, obeyed the voice of the LORD their God, and the words of Haggai the prophet, as the LORD their God had sent him. And the people feared the LORD. Then Haggai, the messenger of the LORD, spoke to the people with the LORD's message, "I am with you, declares the LORD." And the LORD stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people. And they came and worked on the house of the LORD of hosts, their God, on the twenty-fourth day of the month, in the sixth month, in the second year of Darius the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole community obeys, and God answers with his presence and stirs up their will to work.

Obeyed the voice of the LORD their God. Here is something rare in the prophets: people listen. Haggai preached one short sermon, and the governor, the high priest and “all the remnant of the people” obeyed. No argument, no committee. They obeyed both “the voice of the LORD” and “the words of Haggai the prophet”, because God’s word came to them through a man’s words.

And the people feared the LORD. Note the order: they obeyed, and the people feared the LORD. Obedience deepened their reverence. We often wait to feel more before we act; doing what God says is frequently the road to feeling rightly about him.

All the remnant of the people. God calls them “the remnant”, the survivors through whom he keeps his promises. This was a small, poor community with a half-built temple, and they were the people of God in the world at that moment.

I am with you, declares the LORD. Two words in Hebrew, and they are God’s gift to his returning people. Not success, not an easy task, but something better.

The LORD stirred up the spirit. Look carefully at who does what. The people obeyed, and it was a real decision for which they were responsible. And the LORD stirred up the spirit of every one of them, as he had once stirred up the spirit of Cyrus to send them home (Ezra 1:1). Scripture holds both together without embarrassment: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13).

On the twenty-fourth day of the month. The sermon came on the first day of the month (v. 1); the building began on the twenty-fourth. Twenty-three days from conviction to action, including gathering the materials. After sixteen years of “not yet”, three weeks.

With you always. This is the promise God keeps making through the Bible, and it reaches its fulfilment in Jesus, whose very name is Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23), and who sends his people out with the words, “behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). His presence is also his people’s strength.

Willingness can be asked for. That is freeing for anyone who feels no enthusiasm for a duty they know is right. The willingness itself can be asked for, and God’s Spirit gives it.
verseByVerse.note: Zerubbabel was governor and grandson of King Jehoiachin; Joshua was high priest.

1.title: Consider Your Ways
1.overview:
Where we are. This is the first of Haggai’s four dated messages, given on the first day of the sixth month in 520 BC. The temple the returned exiles began lies unfinished, its foundation laid and then abandoned (see the introduction).

The message. Put God first, and stop calling disobedience “not yet”. The people’s leaking wages and thin harvests are not bad luck but God’s own voice, calling them to consider where their lives are going. And when they turn and obey, he gives them not prosperity first but himself: “I am with you” (v. 13). He even supplies the willingness to obey, by stirring up their spirit.

Why it was said. The returned community was small, poor and opposed by its neighbours, and it had decided that rebuilding could wait for better times (see the introduction). Meanwhile its own homes had been finished. Haggai speaks to the governor, the high priest and the people together, because the delay belonged to all of them.

How the chapter makes its case. God quotes their excuse, “the time has not yet come”, and sets it beside their panelled houses and his ruined one (vv. 1–4). He calls them to consider their ways: much sown, little harvested, wages dropped into “a bag with holes” (vv. 5–6). Then the command, go up, bring wood and build, for his pleasure and glory, and the explanation: he has withheld the dew because each of them is busy with his own house (vv. 7–11). Leaders and people obey and fear the LORD; he answers, “I am with you”, stirs up their spirit, and twenty-three days later they are at work (vv. 12–15).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. The temple was where God chose to dwell among his people; in Jesus he came to dwell in person, and Jesus spoke of his own body as the temple (John 2:19–21). The people put their own houses first, but one man was wholly given to his Father’s house: “Zeal for your house will consume me” (John 2:17). And the promise “I am with you” is the name of Jesus himself, Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23), who says to his people, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

For us. A church building is not God’s house today; his people are (1 Corinthians 3:16). But Haggai still asks where our first time, money and strength actually go, and exposes our favourite word, “later”. The honest look is safe for those who belong to Christ, for the God who says “Consider your ways” also says “I am with you”, and he gives the will to obey to those who ask him.
1.theology:
Most disobedience is postponement rather than refusal: "the time has not yet come" (v. 2).

Our real priorities are shown by where our time and money actually go (v. 4).

God calls his people to stop and consider the direction of their lives before he tells them what to do (vv. 5, 7).

God may speak through frustrated circumstances, though not every hardship is a specific judgment (vv. 6, 9-11).

God's house exists for his pleasure and glory, not for our convenience (v. 8).

Reverence does not always come before obedience; often it grows out of it (v. 12).

God's promise to his obedient people is his presence, which is also their strength (v. 13; Matt 28:20).

God stirs up the will of his people, and his people genuinely act (v. 14).
1.examples:
For sixteen years a building site stood untouched, with panelled walls at home and rubble at the temple, while each month's wages dropped into a bag with holes in it and God called for a drought the way a master calls a servant.

Then one short sermon, and a whole community obeyed it. God answered with four words, I am with you, and twenty-three days later the first loads of timber arrived.

keyVerse.quote: Then Haggai, the messenger of the LORD, spoke to the people with the LORD’s message, “I am with you, declares the LORD.”
keyVerse.note: The chapter turns on this verse. After the rebuke and the people’s obedience, God gives them neither a reward nor an easy task, but himself, and that presence is what carries them into the work. It is the promise that runs through the whole Bible and is fulfilled in Jesus, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23).

1.reflection:
“These people say the time has not yet come” (v. 2). What are some of the things God has asked of you, or of your church, that tend to be labelled “not yet”, and what usually lies behind the delay?

God says, “Consider your ways” (vv. 5, 7). If someone read your diary and your bank statement for the past month, what would they conclude about your real priorities, and how can we look at that honestly without either excuses or despair?

Haggai says God was speaking through the people’s failed harvests (vv. 9–11), yet Jesus warns against reading every hardship as a judgment (Luke 13:1–5). How can we tell the difference, and how should we talk about this with someone who is suffering?

The people obeyed, and then “the LORD stirred up the spirit” of them all (vv. 12–14). How does it help to know that God gives the will to obey, and what step of obedience might you ask him for the willingness to take this week?

2.text: <sup>1</sup>In the seventh month, on the twenty-first day of the month, the word of the LORD came by the hand of Haggai the prophet:<sup>2</sup>"Speak now to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and to all the remnant of the people, and say,<sup>3</sup>'Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How do you see it now? Is it not as nothing in your eyes?<sup>4</sup>Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel, declares the LORD. Be strong, O Joshua, son of Jehozadak, the high priest. Be strong, all you people of the land, declares the LORD. Work, for I am with you, declares the LORD of hosts,<sup>5</sup>according to the covenant that I made with you when you came out of Egypt. verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Be Strong, for I Am with You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers discouragement over small beginnings not by denying it but with his presence, his Spirit and a promise of greater glory. A month into the work he asks the older people who remember Solomon’s temple how this one looks: “Is it not as nothing in your eyes?” (vv. 1–3). Then three times he says “Be strong”, to governor, high priest and people, and adds, “Work, for I am with you”, resting it on his covenant from the exodus and on his Spirit, who remains among them (vv. 4–5). Finally he lifts their eyes: he will shake the heavens and the nations, the silver and gold are his, and “The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former” (vv. 6–9).
verseByVerse.theology: God meets discouragement over small beginnings with his presence, his Spirit and a promise of greater glory.

verseByVerse.quote: In the seventh month, on the twenty-first day of the month, the word of the LORD came by the hand of Haggai the prophet: "Speak now to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and to all the remnant of the people, and say, 'Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How do you see it now? Is it not as nothing in your eyes?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God openly names the old people’s disappointment: beside Solomon’s temple, this one looks like nothing.

Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? A month into the work, the excitement has worn off, and God aims his question at the oldest people in the crowd. Solomon’s temple had been destroyed sixty-six years earlier, so a few men in their seventies and eighties could remember it: the gold, the scale, the glory. Ezra records that when the foundation of this new temple was laid, those same old men “wept with a loud voice” (Ezra 3:12).

In the seventh month, on the twenty-first day. The date sharpened the ache. The twenty-first of the seventh month was the last day of the Feast of Booths, the harvest festival at which Solomon had dedicated the first temple (1 Kings 8:2), and this year there was little harvest to celebrate (1:10–11).

Is it not as nothing in your eyes? God does not argue with their disappointment; he states it. The new building genuinely was poor beside what had stood there. Every church that remembers better days knows this feeling, and so does every believer whose present walk with God seems thin compared with an earlier season.

Something better to look at. Comparing the present with the past can be honest and still paralyse us. God does not talk the people out of their memory; he gives them something better to look at (vv. 4–9).

verseByVerse.quote: Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel, declares the LORD. Be strong, O Joshua, son of Jehozadak, the high priest. Be strong, all you people of the land, declares the LORD. Work, for I am with you, declares the LORD of hosts, according to the covenant that I made with you when you came out of Egypt. My Spirit remains in your midst. Fear not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers discouragement with “Be strong” and “Work”, grounded in his covenant presence and his Spirit among them.

Be strong. Three times, to governor, high priest and every ordinary person on the site. The words echo David’s charge to Solomon for the first temple, “Be strong and courageous and do it” (1 Chronicles 28:20), and God’s charge to Joshua son of Nun (Joshua 1:6–9): the second temple is built with the same courage and promise as the first.

Work, for I am with you. Courage is followed by a command: not wait for better circumstances, but carry on with the job in front of you. And the reason, repeated from 1:13: “for I am with you”.

According to the covenant. The ground of it all is “the covenant that I made with you when you came out of Egypt”, centuries before. God’s commitments do not expire.

My Spirit remains in your midst. The little community had no ark, no visible glory and a half-built temple, but it had the Spirit of God. Zechariah, preaching alongside Haggai, said it memorably to the same governor: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (Zechariah 4:6). Many think of the Spirit as a force, or a feeling that comes and goes. Haggai ties him to the exodus, as Isaiah did when he remembered the God who “put in the midst of them his Holy Spirit” (Isaiah 63:11). The Spirit is God himself, personally present with his people, and he had not left. See also God the Holy Spirit in the Theological Dictionary.

Poured out by Jesus. The Spirit who remained in Haggai’s day has now been given in fullness by Jesus. Exalted to the Father’s right hand, he “received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit” and “poured out this” on his people (Acts 2:33), so that every believer is now a dwelling place of God.

Not measured by what we see. The builders measured their strength by what they could see: no gold, no ark, an unimpressive wall. We do the same with budgets, gifts and numbers. But you do not have to feel the Spirit for him to be there. In practice, before the task you feel unequal to, the dull duty or the hard conversation, stop and say, “Your Spirit is here; help me,” and then pick up the tools.

Uncertain wording. The opening of verse 5 is compressed in Hebrew, literally “the word that I cut with you”, using the verb for making a covenant. The ESV takes it as the ground of the command; others as something to remember. Either way, the exodus promise still stands.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD of hosts: Yet once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth and the sea and the dry land. And I will shake all nations, so that the treasures of all nations shall come in, and I will fill this house with glory, says the LORD of hosts. The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, declares the LORD of hosts. The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former, says the LORD of hosts. And in this place I will give peace, declares the LORD of hosts.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will shake creation and the nations and fill this modest house with a glory greater than Solomon’s, a promise kept when Christ came to it.

Yet once more, in a little while, I will shake. God lifts their eyes from the scaffolding to the end of history. He will shake everything: heavens, earth, sea, dry land, and all nations. “Once more” looks back to Sinai, when the earth shook at God’s coming (Exodus 19:18), and Hebrews makes the link: “At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, ‘Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens’” (Hebrews 12:26). “In a little while” is God’s reckoning: the promise began to be kept five centuries later.

The silver is mine, and the gold is mine. A word for a congregation with no money: all the silver and gold in the world is already God’s. He has never been short of funds, only of willing hands.

The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former. How could this shabby building outshine Solomon’s? In part, it was later enlarged and beautified on a grand scale by Herod, and the wealth of nations did flow into it. But the real answer is a person. Malachi promised that “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple” (Malachi 3:1), and he did. Jesus was carried into these courts as a baby, taught here, and drove out the traders. Solomon’s temple had gold; this one had God in the flesh standing in it. The builders had no idea who would one day stand inside it.

In this place I will give peace. The promise came true in him: angels sang of “peace” at his birth (Luke 2:14), and “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14), the one who reconciles us to God by his cross.

A kingdom that cannot be shaken. Hebrews draws out the meaning of the shaking: it indicates “the removal of things that are shaken”, so that “the things that cannot be shaken may remain”, and Christians are “receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Hebrews 12:27–28). Everything that can be lost will be; what remains is God’s kingdom, and his people belong to it.

Uncertain wording. Is “the treasures of all nations” the Messiah? The Latin Bible (the Vulgate) and the KJV read “the desire of all nations” and took it to mean Christ. The Hebrew noun can be read as singular, but its verb is plural, so most translators read “treasures”, as the ESV has it: the wealth of the nations brought to adorn God’s house (v. 8). Either way, the greater glory came with Christ himself (Luke 2:27–32).
verseByVerse.note: Herod began rebuilding the temple about 20 BC, and the work went on for decades (compare John 2:20).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–19 — Holy, Unclean, and Blessed from This Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Religious activity cannot make anyone holy, but God blesses his people from the day they turn to him. Haggai asks the priests two questions about the law: holy meat carried in a garment does not make other food holy, but a person made unclean by a dead body makes everything he touches unclean (vv. 10–13). So it is with this people and their offerings (v. 14). Then he asks them to remember the years of neglect, half harvests, blight and hail, and “yet you did not turn to me” (vv. 15–17). Now, with the barns still empty and the trees bare, God says, “from this day on I will bless you” (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: Holiness is not caught by contact with holy things; but God blesses from the day his people begin to obey.

verseByVerse.quote: On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came by Haggai the prophet, "Thus says the LORD of hosts: Ask the priests about the law: 'If someone carries holy meat in the fold of his garment and touches with his fold bread or stew or wine or oil or any kind of food, does it become holy?'" The priests answered and said, "No." Then Haggai said, "If someone who is unclean by contact with a dead body touches any of these, does it become unclean?" The priests answered and said, "It does become unclean." Then Haggai answered and said, "So is it with this people, and with this nation before me, declares the LORD, and so with every work of their hands. And what they offer there is unclean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Holiness does not pass by contact but uncleanness does, so handling sacred things cannot make an unclean people clean.

Ask the priests about the law. Two months later Haggai asks the priests two technical questions about the law, and they answer correctly. The first: does holiness spread by contact? If a man carries consecrated meat in the fold of his robe and the robe brushes some bread, is the bread now holy? “No.” The second: does uncleanness spread? If a man who has touched a corpse touches food, is the food unclean? “It does become unclean” (Numbers 19:22).

Uncleanness is contagious. That is the sober lesson: uncleanness spreads; holiness does not. Touching holy things makes no one holy.

So is it with this people. The application is unexpected from a prophet who has just got the temple started: restarting the building does not make them clean. Sixteen years of neglect had left a deeper problem than an unfinished wall, and religious activity cannot scrub it out. “What they offer there”, on the altar the returned exiles had set up among the ruins (Ezra 3:2–3), is unclean too.

Why the gospel astonishes. That is exactly what makes the gospel astonishing. Under the law, the clean thing could not cleanse the unclean; the unclean defiled the clean. Then Jesus touched a leper, and the leper was made clean and Jesus was not defiled (Mark 1:41–42). In him the flow runs the other way, because he is not merely holy but the source of holiness.

What it does not mean. This is no argument for avoiding people who do not know God; in Jesus holiness proved stronger than defilement. Nor is it a reason to despair, for the next verses promise blessing. The point is that we cannot make ourselves acceptable by handling sacred things. Church attendance, communion, service on a rota: none of these transfers holiness. Only God can make a person clean, which is why Christ came.

Why do we still want to be clean? Modern people find the purity laws strange (see the note on Leviticus 11:44–45), yet we have not lost the instinct. We talk about clean eating, detoxes, digital cleanses and cutting toxic people out of our lives, sensing rightly that contamination spreads. What our culture lacks is any way of actually being made clean, so we keep scrubbing: another regime, another round of proving we are the good ones. Haggai’s priests would have understood: even the most sacred routine cannot reach the heart. Cleanness with Jesus is not a regime to keep up but a gift received, and it reaches exactly where Haggai said religion could not: “how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Hebrews 9:14). Dead works were the corpse on our hands. He washes even those.

Where Christians differ: who is “this people”? Some have taken it to mean the Samaritans, whose offer to help build had been refused (Ezra 4:1–3). This commentary’s view: it is Judah itself, as most hold, since God used the same words of them in 1:2 and goes straight on to their own harvests (vv. 15–19).
verseByVerse.note: The second question rests on Numbers 19:11-22, where touching a dead body makes a person unclean for seven days.

verseByVerse.quote: Now then, consider from this day onward. Before stone was placed upon stone in the temple of the LORD, how did you fare? When one came to a heap of twenty measures, there were but ten. When one came to the wine vat to draw fifty measures, there were but twenty. I struck you and all the products of your toil with blight and with mildew and with hail, yet you did not turn to me, declares the LORD. Consider from this day onward, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month. Since the day that the foundation of the LORD's temple was laid, consider: Is the seed yet in the barn? Indeed, the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive tree have yielded nothing. But from this day on I will bless you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember how little the years of neglect produced, says God; and now, with the barns still empty, from this day on I will bless you.

Consider from this day onward. Again the call to consider: look honestly at the years of neglect. A heap of grain that should have measured twenty gave ten; a wine vat that should have yielded fifty gave twenty.

Yet you did not turn to me. The saddest line in the book. Haggai is echoing Amos, almost word for word: “I struck you with blight and mildew… yet you did not return to me” (Amos 4:9), a refrain Amos sounds five times (Amos 4:6–11). God’s discipline is not an end in itself; it is a summons home, and it is possible to endure it without ever hearing it.

Is the seed yet in the barn? Now the turn. The barns are still empty. The vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate and the olive have “yielded nothing”. Nothing visible has changed at all.

But from this day on I will bless you. The date is precise, three months after the work began, and the blessing is announced before there is any evidence of it, so that they must take God at his word. That is how God usually works: the promise first, the harvest later, and in between an empty barn and a full promise.

Between promise and harvest. Christians live in the same gap. The decisive day has come: Christ has died and risen, and every promise of God has its “Yes” in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). The full harvest is still to come, and we wait with “the firstfruits of the Spirit” (Romans 8:23).

Was the foundation not laid in 536 BC (Ezra 3:10)? It was begun then, and the work stopped. Haggai probably means the fresh start of 520, when the foundation work was resumed and properly laid; the Hebrew verb can mean to restore or re-found. The two books describe two stages of the same building.

Uncertain wording. “From this day onward” could also be translated “from this day backward”, as the ESV notes; the Hebrew phrase is used both ways, and Haggai seems to ask them to look back over the lean years and then forward from this day. In verse 17, “yet you did not turn to me” is very compressed in Hebrew, literally “and not you to me”; the ESV fills it out from Amos 4:9.

Textual note. The ESV notes that the Hebrew at the start of verse 16 is difficult, and its reading “how did you fare?” follows the Greek.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God overturns empires and keeps his promise to David’s line, even through an obscure governor of a ruined city. On the same day as the previous message, Haggai receives a word for Zerubbabel alone. God is about to shake heaven and earth, overthrow the thrones of kingdoms, and bring down their chariots and riders, each by his brother’s sword (vv. 20–22). And on that day he will take Zerubbabel, his servant, and make him like a signet ring, “for I have chosen you” (v. 23). The ring that God had torn off Zerubbabel’s grandfather is put back on, a pledge that leads to Christ.
verseByVerse.theology: God overturns empires and keeps his promise to David's line through an obscure governor of a ruined city.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came a second time to Haggai on the twenty-fourth day of the month, "Speak to Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, saying, I am about to shake the heavens and the earth, and to overthrow the throne of kingdoms. I am about to destroy the strength of the kingdoms of the nations, and overthrow the chariots and their riders. And the horses and their riders shall go down, every one by the sword of his brother. On that day, declares the LORD of hosts, I will take you, O Zerubbabel my servant, the son of Shealtiel, declares the LORD, and make you like a signet ring, for I have chosen you, declares the LORD of hosts."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will overthrow the world’s powers and make Zerubbabel, heir of a cast-off royal line, his chosen signet ring: a pledge kept in Christ.

To overthrow the throne of kingdoms. The last message is for one man, the governor of a small, poor Persian province, and it concerns the great powers. God will overthrow their thrones, destroy their strength, and bring down “the horses and their riders” in confusion, “every one by the sword of his brother”. The words recall the exodus, where horse and rider were thrown into the sea (Exodus 15:1), and Gideon’s enemies turning their swords on each other (Judges 7:22). Persia looked permanent. Every empire does, until it does not.

Make you like a signet ring. A signet ring carried a man’s seal; it was how he signed documents and stamped his authority. Handing it over meant trusting someone with your full authority, as Pharaoh did with Joseph (Genesis 41:42). (The ESV notes that the Hebrew reads “the signet ring”.)

The signet ring restored. Now hear what God had said a lifetime earlier about Zerubbabel’s own grandfather, the king of Judah carried into exile: “though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were the signet ring on my right hand, yet I would tear you off” (Jeremiah 22:24). The royal ring had been pulled off and thrown away. Here God takes the grandson of that rejected king and makes him like a signet ring again.

My servant … I have chosen you. These are royal words, the language God used of David: “He chose David his servant” (Psalm 78:70). So the book that began with people saying “the time has not yet come” ends with God saying “I have chosen you”. What looks small in our hands is where God does his largest work.

In the genealogy of Jesus. Zerubbabel appears in the genealogy of Jesus: “Shealtiel the father of Zerubbabel”, and on down the line to “Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born” (Matthew 1:12–16). The promise to David ran through this obscure governor, rebuilding a modest temple in a ruined city, and arrived at Christ.

Was Zerubbabel really Jehoiachin’s grandson? Ezra, Haggai and Matthew call him the son of Shealtiel; 1 Chronicles 3:17–19 makes him the son of Shealtiel’s brother Pedaiah, perhaps by adoption or a levirate marriage (a man raising children for a brother who died childless). Either way, he was Jehoiachin’s grandson.

Had not Jeremiah said none of Jehoiachin’s offspring would sit on David’s throne (Jeremiah 22:30)? Zerubbabel never did. He was a governor, and we hear no more of him after the temple. The ring was a pledge that God had not finished with David’s line; the throne was kept for a greater son (see the introduction).

When is the shaking of the nations? Not in Zerubbabel’s day, for Persia stood. It is God’s long work of overturning kingdoms, begun in Christ and completed at his return.
verseByVerse.note: Zechariah, preaching at the same time, promised that the hands of Zerubbabel which laid the foundation would also complete the house (Zech 4:9).

2.title: The Latter Glory of This House
2.overview:
Where we are. In chapter 1 the people obeyed, God said “I am with you”, and work on the temple began. Chapter 2 holds Haggai’s last three messages, spread over the next three months of 520 BC.

The message. Do not measure God’s work by what you can see. The new temple looks like nothing, but God is with his people by his covenant and his Spirit, and he will fill this house with a glory greater than Solomon’s. Their work cannot make them holy, for uncleanness spreads and holiness does not; yet God blesses them from the day they obey, before there is any harvest to show for it. And the line of David, which seemed thrown away, is still his chosen signet ring.

Why it was said. The excitement of starting had worn off. The older people remembered Solomon’s temple and wept over this one, harvests were still poor, and Judah was a tiny province in an empire that looked permanent (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God names the old people’s disappointment, “Is it not as nothing in your eyes?” (vv. 1–3), then answers it: “Be strong… Work, for I am with you”, because his covenant stands and his Spirit remains among them (vv. 4–5). He will shake heaven, earth and nations, and “The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former” (vv. 6–9). Two questions to the priests show that holiness does not pass by touch but uncleanness does, so this people and their offerings are unclean (vv. 10–14). Yet, though the barns are empty, “from this day on I will bless you” (vv. 15–19). Last, God will overthrow the thrones of kingdoms and make Zerubbabel “like a signet ring, for I have chosen you” (vv. 20–23).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise above all. The greater glory came when the Lord himself entered this temple in Jesus (Malachi 3:1; Luke 2:27–32). The peace promised “in this place” is the peace he made, for “he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14). The chapter also exposes a need: no sacred routine can make the unclean clean, but Jesus touched the unclean and made them whole. And the signet ring passed from Zerubbabel down David’s line to Jesus (Matthew 1:12–16), in whom God keeps every promise.

For us. When God’s work looks small, measure it by his presence and his promise, not by appearances, and keep working. Do not trust your religious activity to make you clean; only Christ can do that. And live by God’s word in the gap between promise and harvest, because everything that can be shaken will be, but we are “receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Hebrews 12:28).
2.theology:
God does not deny our disappointment over small beginnings; he answers it with his presence and his promise (vv. 3-5).

Courage and work belong together, grounded in covenant and in the Spirit who remains among God's people (vv. 4-5; Zech 4:6).

Everything that can be shaken will be; only God's kingdom remains (vv. 6-7; Heb 12:26-28).

God owns all the wealth there is; his work is never short of resources, only of willing hands (v. 8).

The glory of the second temple was that Christ stood in it, and the peace promised there is the peace he made (v. 9; Mal 3:1; Eph 2:14).

Holiness is not transferred by contact with holy things; only God can cleanse a person (vv. 11-14; Num 19:22).

God's discipline is a summons home, and it can be endured without being heard (v. 17; Amos 4:6-11).

God announces blessing before there is any evidence of it, so that his people live by his word (vv. 18-19).

God overturns empires and keeps his promise to David's line through obscure people, all the way to Christ (vv. 21-23; Jer 22:24; Matt 1:12).
2.examples:
Old men weep at a foundation because they remember something better, and God answers with "Be strong" three times on one building site. A congregation with no money is told that all the gold is his already, and a shabby temple is promised a glory it cannot imagine: one day God will stand in it.

Then two questions to the priests teach that uncleanness is catching and holiness is not, a blessing is promised on a day when the barns are still empty, and a signet ring torn off a grandfather is given back to his grandson.

keyVerse.quote: The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former, says the LORD of hosts. And in this place I will give peace, declares the LORD of hosts.
keyVerse.note: Spoken to people who thought their temple was “as nothing” (v. 3), this promise turns the chapter from discouragement to hope. It was not kept by gold, for the rebuilt temple never matched Solomon’s, but by the Lord himself coming to it in Jesus, who is “our peace” (Ephesians 2:14).

2.reflection:
The old people looked at the new temple and found it “as nothing” (v. 3). When have you compared your church or your own walk with God unfavourably with the past, and how do God’s words in verses 4–5 speak to that?

God’s answer to discouragement is “Be strong… Work, for I am with you” and “My Spirit remains in your midst” (vv. 4–5). What task are you facing that feels too big or too dull, and what difference would it make to begin it by remembering that the Spirit is present?

Haggai’s priests confirm that holiness does not spread by touch but uncleanness does (vv. 11–14). What religious habits are we tempted to rely on to make us acceptable to God, and why is it good news that Jesus touched the unclean and made them clean?

God promised blessing while the barns were still empty (vv. 18–19). Where are you waiting between God’s promise and its fulfilment, and how can we help one another keep trusting his word in that gap?
